human_tolerance.notes: 'Often they live in close association with man, often under the floors of outbuildings, and even live successfully on the fringe of suburbia. When habituated to human presence, they may tolerate close approach.' The article also notes they are often spotted by humans when crossing roads, hence High road_mortality.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Litters of one to three young are born from August to December, hidden in burrows, rock crevices or tree hollows.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Outside the breeding season the species is solitary and lives in overlapping home ranges; the source does not state whether it is territorial.

taxonomy.note: GBIF's backbone accepts Galerella pulverulenta and lists Herpestes pulverulentus, the name the Wikipedia article uses, as a synonym; the schema asks for the name the GBIF backbone accepts, so Galerella pulverulenta is used here.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 5219126 from the species/match endpoint and iNaturalist taxon 74413, which iNaturalist lists under the synonym Herpestes pulverulentus. The Wikidata QID is the one the English article's taxobox links to.

conservation.note: The species article's taxobox records IUCN category Least Concern.

range.note: 'a small mammal native to South Africa, Lesotho and southern Namibia' gives the three native countries, and the Distribution section adds that it occurs in much of the rest of South Africa and in the west northwards to southern Angola without being found in the grassland biome.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Walk follows from ground foraging: insects 'are caught on the ground and then held down with the forefeet', and larger prey is stalked and killed with a bite to the head. Climb follows from the species sheltering in 'hollows in tree trunks'.

traits.nest_type.note: Litters are 'hidden in burrows, rock crevices or tree hollows', which is Cavity rather than a burrow this species digs itself: 'They are poor diggers so they utilize piles of rocks, crevices, deserted burrows and hollows in tree trunks for shelter'.

traits.perching.note: A ground-foraging terrestrial carnivore; the article describes sheltering in tree hollows but no climbing behaviour, so no perching is recorded.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of the sourced 0.5 to 1.0 kg range.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Honest gap. Neither the species article, Wikidata nor GBIF gives a longevity figure for this species, and no openly licensed source with one was found. 8 years is an authored placeholder for a small mongoose; it is not a sourced value.

traits.home_range_ha.note: 'They live in overlapping home ranges of 5-68 ha, with the males having larger ranges than the females.' The midpoint, 36 ha, is recorded.

traits.diet.note: 'The Cape grey mongoose feeds mostly on insects and small rodents, but will also eat birds, small reptiles, amphibians, other invertebrates, and fruit. They have been known to eat carrion and garbage as well', and 'it is predominantly insectivorous but also carnivorous ... Small rodents, in particular Otomys and Rhabdomys, are their most important dietary component.' The 0.5 vertebrate / 0.35 invertebrate / 0.1 fruit / 0.05 carrion split is authored, with the low carrion share reflecting 'have been known to'; the source gives no proportions.

traits.senses.note: Authored for an insectivorous carnivore that stalks and kills prey: high olfaction, coloured vision, moderate hearing.

traits.social.note: 'When not breeding, it is solitary, but litter remains together in a family party at least until late adolescence.' The upper bound of 5 covers a family party of the one to three young the article gives.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'The Cape grey mongoose is diurnal.' This corrects an assumption that a small mongoose in a warm climate would be nocturnal; the sourced record is what this field carries.

traits.defense.note: Honest gap with a judgement. The article does not describe this species' response to a threat. Flee is recorded for a small carnivore that is 'often spotted by humans when they cross roads' and that uses cover rather than confrontation.

traits.wariness.note: 'When habituated to human presence, they may tolerate close approach', and the species lives under the floors of outbuildings and on the fringe of suburbia.

habitat.use.note: Almost entirely terrestrial: prey is caught on the ground and held down with the forefeet, and the species shelters in crevices and tree hollows. The 0.9 ground / 0.1 arboreal split is authored from that.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: 'They are poor diggers so they utilize piles of rocks, crevices, deserted burrows and hollows in tree trunks for shelter when there is not sufficient bush cover.'

habitat.resources.note: small_vertebrate, invertebrate, fruit and carrion map one to one onto the diet paragraph; cavity follows the shelter sentence and burrow the breeding-hiding sentence. Weights are authored.

habitat.density_per_ha.note: 'Its density in areas where the species is established, ranges from one mongoose per 60 hectares to one per two hectares' gives min 1/60 = 0.017 and max 1/2 = 0.5 per hectare. The source gives no mode, so typical is authored as 0.1 within the sourced bounds.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Exploiter, dist_building_min_m, light_max, uses_gardens and road_mortality are all sourced from the Habitat and Behaviour sections, including the two passages on living under outbuilding floors, on the fringe of suburbia, tolerating close approach when habituated, and being spotted crossing roads. impervious_max is authored.

seasonal.strategy.note: The species is described as present year-round in a wide range of habitats with a defined August to December breeding window and no migration or dormancy, so ActiveYearRound is recorded.

seasonal.phases.note: 'Litters of 1-3 young are born from August to December' gives the breeding window; the solitary non-breeding behaviour is also stated. The non-breeding window and its 'territorial' label are authored, the article noting it is 'not entirely clear whether this species is territorial'.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'At birth, the pups are fully furred but their eyes and ears are closed, only opening after about a fortnight', and 'the young remain in the breeding burrow until they are fully weaned'. The 60-day duration and 0.5 scale are authored; no weaning age is given.

look.note: 'It is a dark grey colour with a darker tip of the tail. The legs are a darker grey than the rest of the body. It has a typical elongated mongoose body-shape. The ears are small and rounded and are situated on the sides of the head. The tail is long and bushy.' Proportions are authored.

behavior.note: Mostly authored for the shared ground-forager program, which the article's behaviour supports directly: 'Insects and other arthropoda such as spiders are caught on the ground', it stalks and kills rodents, is diurnal, and shelters in cover. flee_m, calm_m, food_m and the daylight rest window are authored from that.
